title: [round · deployment-engineer shape] 45 minutes: retrieval over classified documents
body:
> **Simulated interview round.** A full loop in the shape a forward-deployed / deployment-engineer
> panel actually runs, with the rubric attached. Written for teaching; the numbers and the
> failure modes are from this repository.

## The prompt, as it would be given

> *"Your client's analysts search a document store. Every paragraph carries a classification
> marking, and markings differ **within** a single document. An analyst must never see a
> paragraph above their clearance — and must never be able to infer its existence from the
> system's behaviour. The ontology of markings changes weekly. You have four weeks and one of
> their engineers. Design it."*

## What this shape is really testing

Not retrieval. **Whether you notice that the hard constraint is not the retrieval problem.**

Three things a panel of this kind is scoring:

1. Do you ask about the *inference* channel, or only the *access* channel?
2. Do you treat a weekly-changing ontology as a data-model problem or wave at it?
3. Do you say what you would do in week one versus week four, or design the finished system?

## The 45 minutes, roughly

| Minutes | What happens |
|---|---|
| 0–5 | Clarifying questions. **This is scored.** |
| 5–20 | Your design, out loud |
| 20–35 | Pressure on one weak point they have already chosen |
| 35–42 | "What would you do in week one?" |
| 42–45 | Your questions |

## The clarifying questions worth asking

- **"Can an analyst know that a document exists but is above their clearance?"** This is the
  whole question. If no, result counts, latency and even "no results" are inference channels.
- "Is the marking on the paragraph, or derived from the document plus the paragraph?"
- "When a marking is *downgraded*, does that apply retroactively to indexed content?"
- "What is the audit requirement — do you need to reconstruct who could see what, on a past date?"

## The trap

Almost everyone proposes **post-filtering**: retrieve, then drop what the analyst may not see.

It is wrong twice. It collapses `k` unpredictably — ask for 10, get 3, with no signal that
happened. And it is an **inference channel**: the number of results is a function of content the
analyst cannot see. Ask for a rare term, get 2 results instead of 10, and you have learned that
8 classified paragraphs mention it.

**Pre-filter inside the retrieval query.** In this repo that is
`store.lexical(..., acl_groups=...)`, filtering in SQL rather than after it, and it is why
`k_collapse` is a field in the trace.

comments.body:
> **Rafael** · cohort peer · came from search infra

Adding the second-order version of the trap, because a good panel goes here and it is where I
have seen strong candidates fall over.

You pre-filter correctly, so result counts are clean. **Latency is not.** A query that touches a
large classified region does more index work and comes back slower, and a patient adversary can
read that. In an environment that cares about this at all, they will ask.

The answers are constant-time padding or a fixed latency floor, both of which cost real
performance — and the right move in the interview is to **name the trade rather than solve it**.
"Here is a channel, here is what closing it costs, this is a decision for your security team, not
for me on a whiteboard" scores better than a confident fix.

replies.body:
> **Priya** · cohort peer

Also worth saying out loud that the ANN path needs separate treatment. Pre-filtering by deleting
nodes from the graph can **disconnect** the region containing the answer — that is
[#2](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/issues/2) — so "we pre-filter" is not one design,
it is a different design for the exact and approximate paths.

comments.body:
Marking this as the answer — the model response, plus the rubric.

---

**A strong answer, roughly as I would give it.**

> "Before designing I need one thing: **can an analyst know a document exists but is above their
> clearance?** If not, this is not an access-control problem, it is an inference-channel problem,
> and it changes the design.
>
> Assuming not. **Markings go on the chunk, denormalised, and the filter goes inside the
> retrieval query** — never after it. Post-filtering collapses `k` unpredictably and leaks: result
> count becomes a function of content you cannot see.
>
> Because the ontology changes weekly, chunks carry a **group key**, not a marking set. The
> mapping from analyst to permitted keys lives in a small, fast store resolved at query time, and
> **it is versioned** — when audit asks in six months who could see what on 3 March, you need the
> mapping as it was, not as it is.
>
> The approximate path needs its own treatment: filtering by removing nodes can disconnect the
> graph, so either filter-aware traversal or exact search inside a permitted subset, chosen on
> measured recall rather than assumed.
>
> **Week one is not any of that.** Week one is an eval set with clearance levels as a first-class
> slice, and a permission-isolation test in CI that fails the build if a single chunk crosses a
> boundary. I would not ship a retrieval change before that exists, because there would be no way
> to know I had broken it."

---

## How this is scored

| Signal | Weak | Strong |
|---|---|---|
| **Clarifying** | Starts designing | Asks the existence-inference question first |
| **The trap** | Post-filter | Pre-filter, and names *both* reasons |
| **Ontology churn** | Rewrite markings on change | Group key + versioned mapping |
| **Audit** | Not mentioned | Versioned mapping, because someone will ask about a past date |
| **Sequencing** | Designs the finished system | Names what week one is, and it is the test |
| **Honesty** | Confident fix for the latency channel | Names the channel, names the cost, hands the decision back |

**The single highest-scoring move** is putting the isolation test before the retrieval work.
Almost nobody does it, and in a regulated context it is the only part of the answer that is
non-negotiable.

Practise: [EX-10](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/blob/main/docs/30-learning/exercises/ex-10-prove-permission-isolation.md)
is this, in code. The design argument is
[#34](https://github.com/akash-coded/nanorag/discussions/34).
